content: Genital warts are soft, wart-like growths that appear on the skin and mucous membranes of the genital area in both men and women. They are a type of sexually transmitted infection (STI). Symptoms of Genital Warts: Genital warts can be raised or flat and are typically flesh-colored. They may resemble cauliflower-like growths. In some cases, they are so small and flat that they are not visible to the naked eye. Common locations for genital warts include: In females: Inside or around the vagina or anus, on the skin surrounding these areas, or on the cervix. In males: On the penis, scrotum, groin area, thighs, or inside and around the anus (especially in those who engage in anal intercourse). In both sexes: On the lips, mouth, tongue, palate, or throat (larynx). Other symptoms, though rare, may include: Increased moisture in the area of the growths. Increased vaginal discharge. Itching of the penis, scrotum, anal area, or vulva. Vaginal bleeding during or after sexual intercourse. Causes of Genital Warts: Genital warts are caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV). There are over 70 different types of HPV. Certain types of HPV cause genital warts, which can appear on the penis, vulva, urethra, vagina, cervix, larynx, and around or inside the anus. Other types of HPV cause common or flat warts on other parts of the body, such as the hands. However, these types do not cause genital warts. HPV infection around the genitals is common, and many people may not exhibit symptoms. Even if asymptomatic, treatment is necessary to prevent complications and transmission to others. In women, HPV can invade the walls of the vagina and cervix. These warts are often flat and not easily visible without specialized procedures. Certain high-risk types of HPV can lead to precancerous changes in the cervix, cervical cancer, or anal cancer. Transmission of HPV and Genital Warts: HPV is transmitted through sexual contact involving the skin or mucous membranes of the anus, mouth, or vagina. Genital warts and HPV can spread even when no visible warts are present. Warts may not appear for 6 weeks to 6 months after infection, and in some cases, it may take years. Therefore, the appearance of warts does not necessarily indicate recent sexual contact outside of a relationship. Not everyone exposed to HPV or genital warts will develop them. Risk Factors for Genital Warts: Having multiple sexual partners. Not knowing the STI status of sexual partners. Becoming sexually active at an early age. Using tobacco and alcohol. Experiencing stress or having other viral infections (e.g., herpes) simultaneously. Being pregnant. Having a weakened immune system, such as during cancer treatment or with AIDS. In children, genital warts may indicate sexual abuse. When to Seek Medical Care: If a current or past sexual partner has genital warts. If you notice visible warts on your external genitals, experience itching, discharge, or abnormal vaginal bleeding. If you suspect a young child may have genital warts. Women should begin Pap smears at age 21. Diagnosis: Genital warts may appear as flesh-colored to white, flat or raised, single or clustered growths on the genitals. In women, a pelvic examination may reveal growths on the vaginal walls or cervix. Magnification (colposcopy) may be used to detect lesions invisible to the naked eye. Applying acetic acid (dilute vinegar) to the tissue can make warts more visible. A Pap smear may detect changes caused by HPV. Women with such changes may require more frequent Pap smears. An HPV DNA test can identify high-risk HPV types associated with cervical cancer. This test may be done as a screening for women over 30 or for women of any age with slightly abnormal Pap test results. Treatment Options: Genital warts must be treated by a healthcare provider. Over-the-counter remedies for other types of warts should not be used. Treatment options include: Topical treatments applied by a doctor or prescribed for home use, such as: Imiquimod (Aldara) Podophyllin and podofilox (Condylox) Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) Surgical treatments, such as: Cryosurgery (freezing the warts) Electrocauterization (burning the warts) Laser therapy Surgical excision (cutting the warts out) All sexual partners must be examined and treated if genital warts are found. Follow-up examinations are necessary to monitor for recurrence. Women with a history of genital warts or whose partners have had genital warts should have annual Pap smears. For warts on the cervix, Pap smears may be needed every 3 to 6 months after initial treatment. Women with precancerous changes caused by HPV may require additional treatment. Vaccination against HPV is recommended for girls and women aged 9 to 26. Prevention: Total abstinence is the only foolproof way to avoid genital warts and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Reducing the number of sexual partners and engaging in a monogamous relationship with a disease-free partner can lower the risk. Male and female condoms reduce the risk of HPV transmission but do not provide complete protection, as the virus can be present on uncovered skin. HPV can be transmitted even when no visible warts or symptoms are present. Vaccines are available to protect against four HPV types that cause most cervical cancers in women. The vaccine is administered as a series of three shots and is recommended for girls and women aged 9 to 26. Prognosis: Most sexually active young women become infected with HPV, but in many cases, the virus resolves on its own. Most men infected with HPV do not develop symptoms or complications but can still transmit the virus to sexual partners. Even after treatment, individuals with genital warts may still infect others. Certain types of genital warts increase the risk of cervical and vulvar cancer in women. Complications: Some HPV types are the primary cause of cervical cancer and vulvar cancer. The types of HPV that cause genital warts are not the same as those that cause penile or anal cancer. Warts may become numerous and large, requiring extensive treatment and follow-up. Prevention and Vaccination: Abstinence and safe sexual practices are key to prevention. Vaccination against HPV is highly recommended for young women and girls aged 9 to 26.
